newsitem.title: USA: Clinton calls for educational standards.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls for educational standards.

text.p: President Clinton took his crusade to improve education on the road Monday, using the historic Maryland State House as a bully pulpit to warn against letting "hide-and-seek excuses" stand in the way of national learning achievement tests.

"The most important thing we can do in education is to hold our students to high standards," Clinton said, while criticising local school boards who oppose national standards on the grounds that they constitute federal interference.

Speaking at the nation's oldest state capital building that been continually in service, Clinton tried to drum up support for his plan to develop national reading tests for fourth graders and national math tests for eighth graders.

"(To) anybody who says that a country as big and diverse as ours can't possibly have national standards ... I say from Maryland to Michigan to Montana, reading is reading and math is math," he said. "No school board is in charge of algebra and no state legislature can enact the laws of physics.

"No matter how much flexibility you have, sooner or later your children are going to have to face the fact that they either can read or they can't; they either can do math or they can't; they know algebra or they don't," Clinton added.
"And if we play around with all these games and hide-and-seek excuses, in the end the only people that will be hurt are those kids, and the rest of the country will pay the price from now on."

His speech was the latest in a series Clinton has made on education since he began his second term Jan. 20. In his State of the Union speech last week he said making the U.S. education system second to none would be his top priority over the next four years.
In what appeared to be a carefully coordinated effort to boost his proposals, he said an industry trade group, the Business Roundtable, had endorsed his standards effort.

"These tests will provide a national benchmark in reading and an international benchmark in mathematics that parents and educators can use to learn how their own children and students are performing," the Business Roundtable said in a statement.

The Maryland State Board of Education also released a statement saying the state was interested in pursing the president's idea for such tests and was "ready to accept the challenge to determine how our students measure up."

In his remarks, Clinton also touched on the subject of welfare, exhorting business and state and local governments to help implement last year's welfare law and to help find jobs for recipients. The law ended the 61-year federal entitlement to welfare, limiting benefits to five years and requiring most recipients to work after two years.
In a day on which Clinton reprised many of the themes that he struck during last year's presidential race, there were also other reminders of his zest for campaigning.
After his speech, Clinton went shopping for Valentine's Day gifts for wife Hillary and daughter Chelsea on a street near the statehouse lined with boutiques and coffeehouses.

He shook hands with hundreds of onlookers, stopping often to pose for pictures and sign autographs. Clinton became so engrossed in political activity he was three hours late getting back to the White House.
